repairs.value: Harris argues that possible conscious minds, including suffering computers and morally altered humans, extend moral concern beyond anthropocentric truths while preserving suffering as a shared evaluative basis.
repairs.rationale: This complete condensation accurately joins Harris’s possible-minds examples to his cross-species evaluative claim without expanding the frozen judgment.

repairs.value: Strongest feature: Harris directly answers Haidt’s anthropocentric account by extending moral consideration to artificial or biologically transformed consciousness, while his invariant comparison of otherwise equivalent misery supplies a coherent cross-species criterion. Principal limitation: These counterfactual cases establish conceptual reach, not the stronger conclusion that every moral category, institutional obligation, or disagreement can be exhaustively reduced to suffering and flourishing without additional normative argument. Live burden: Harris must explain why conscious experience provides sufficient guidance across competing goods and complex tradeoffs, while preserving the limited force of Haidt’s concession that more misery is worse, other-things-equal. Locked score: The 87-point assessment appropriately rewards exceptional responsiveness, strong coherence, and clear motion-level relevance, yet withholds stronger endorsement because imaginative possibilities illuminate scope more securely than they justify comprehensive sufficiency.
repairs.rationale: This four-sentence assessment identifies the reply’s precise achievement and unresolved sufficiency burden while explicitly preserving the locked score and concessions.
